diagnosis.what_is_wrong: No kernel evidence establishes a fault causing the coding task to run slowly. The trace begins during a high-activity burst and shows a sharp fall in runnable-work generation at about 03:24:08.300, but the recording has no pre-burst baseline and the fall is not evidence of CPU starvation or a host resource failure; the reported task slowdown cannot be confirmed or rejected from this short trace.
diagnosis.evidence: Used the recorded ctf_timespan/proclife findings to establish the 03:24:07.500–03:24:26.200 recording and that the claude/Bun workload remained present in the sole observed pid_ns 4026531836, with no in-trace turnover. Compared the matched 0.8-second windows from run_python: at 03:24:08.300 sched_wakeup and sched_switch each fell 84.5%, sched_stat_runtime event count fell 84.6%, and aggregate runtime fell 80.7%. Other summaries show the activity drop and no sustained block-I/O elevation; CPU time later rises, largely in python3, without evidence of a competing container. The check that would falsify the benign workload-phase interpretation is evidence of growing wakeup-to-run delay, sustained block-request latency, or a workload/dependency stall across the transition; the supplied notes do not provide those measurements or inspectable raw block lines. Thus the task-duration symptom is not verifiable from these kernel data, and the synchronized count drop alone does not identify a fault.
diagnosis.window_evidence: The only sharp boundary supported by the recorded counts is the activity collapse around 03:24:08.300 (matched windows 03:24:07.500–08.300 and 08.300–09.100). However, because recording begins within the burst and there is no evidence that this transition marks a fault rather than workload completion/idle behavior, it cannot be honestly reported as an incident window.
